extracted.subtask_description: A practical guide to working out and writing undergraduate real-analysis proofs by applying a small set of procedural moves and conventions so that proofs are understandable rather than magical. Emphasises exposing the sequence of routine steps and using expanded definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core philosophy: aim for understanding over memorisation
rubrics_metrics.description: Analysis proofs follow predictable patterns; the right goal is understanding rather than memorising tricks — 'You just keep doing the obvious thing except that from time to time the next step isn't obvious.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat proofs as sequences of standard moves; prefer explaining why each routine step is taken so readers can follow rather than presenting the proof as an inspired leap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let move (prove 'for all x, P(x)')
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove 'for all x, P(x)', write 'Let x be arbitrary' and shift the goal to proving P(x) for that arbitrary x.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use to convert universal statements into a fixed-but-arbitrary object. Anti-pattern: implicitly assuming special properties of x without stating arbitrariness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naming move (when something exists, give it a name)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the statement claims the existence of an object, name that object (e.g., given a convergent subsequence, name its limit a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Naming clarifies references and enables substitution and further manipulation. Anti-pattern: repeatedly referring vaguely to 'the limit' without naming it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expansion (unpack definitions into formal quantifiers)
rubrics_metrics.description: When high-level arguments don't work, unpack definitions into their formal, quantifier-laden form (for example, replace 'convergent' with the ε–N definition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use expansion to convert vague or informal claims into explicit inequalities and quantifiers that can be manipulated. Example: write out 'for every ε>0 there exists N...' rather than relying on intuition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitution into hypotheses (use ∀ to instantiate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a hypothesis of the form ∀u P(u), substitute any specific object x to obtain P(x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard logical instantiation used to derive concrete facts from universal statements. Keep track of scopes and names to avoid clashes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modus ponens (use implications)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given ∀u (P(u) ⇒ Q(u)) and P(x), conclude Q(x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply conditional hypotheses to instantiated facts. Anti-pattern: trying to apply an implication without first ensuring the antecedent holds for the chosen object.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitution into targets (for existential goals)
rubrics_metrics.description: For goals of the form ∃u P(u), pick a promising candidate x and redirect the proof to proving P(x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructive approach: exhibit a witness and then prove it satisfies the required property. Anti-pattern: claiming existence without giving or justifying a witness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triangle inequality and closure moves (combine inequalities strategically)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use inequalities like the triangle inequality (and similar closure properties) to combine intermediate estimates — for example, splitting ε as ε/2 to bridge steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common technique to bound expressions by introducing intermediate terms; use ε/2 or other splits to control sums of errors. Example: estimate |a-b| ≤ |a-c|+|c-b| and bound each term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hallmark: steps follow from expanded definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Manageable proofs consist of steps that follow logically from expanded definitions without introducing novel mathematical objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate proofs by checking that each step can be traced to a definition or a previously established fact. Anti-pattern: leaps that rely on undeclared constructions or hand-waving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hallmark: reasoning is 'non-silly' and sensible
rubrics_metrics.description: The reasoning should remain recognisably sensible — not contrived cleverness or irrelevant detours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer straightforward manipulations over gimmicks; a reader should be able to judge intermediate goals as reasonable. Anti-pattern: convoluted arguments that obscure the central idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hallmark: most moves are procedural, insight is isolated
rubrics_metrics.description: Most steps should be routine procedural moves; only isolated steps should require genuine insight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good exposition separates the single creative insight from the surrounding routine verifications, so readers can follow the flow and identify where the real idea occurs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader's comparative advantage: write to human pattern-recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Humans outperform naive algorithms by understanding English phrasing, recognising obvious simplifications, and judging reasonableness of intermediate goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make use of natural-language explanations and obvious simplifications; present intermediate targets that a human reader can recognise as sensible. Anti-pattern: presenting a solution tailored to a machine-like formalism when clarity for human readers is lost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implication for a 'good proof': expose the move-sequence
rubrics_metrics.description: A good proof in this register exposes its move-sequence so the reader can recognise each step as one of the standard moves, rather than appearing as inspired magic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure proofs so that each step maps to a named or recognisable move (let, naming, expansion, substitution, modus ponens, existential witness, triangle inequality). Explicitly indicate when you are performing a standard move to aid reader comprehension; anti-pattern: compressing many moves into opaque sentences.
